blocks.heading: Market, planned and mixed economies
blocks.text: Economic systems concern how resources are allocated and how production decisions are made. In a market model, private decisions and prices have a major coordinating role. In a planned model, central public decisions direct a substantial part of production and allocation. A mixed economy combines private enterprise with public ownership, provision and regulation. These are models: actual economies differ in the extent and form of intervention. Market economy: advantages are wide consumer choice and a profit motive that encourages efficiency and new products; disadvantages are that people with low incomes may not afford essentials, some services such as street lighting may not be provided, and firms may pollute or gain monopoly power. Planned economy: advantages are that the government can make sure basic needs are met, keep unemployment low and make incomes more equal; disadvantages are little consumer choice, weak incentives to work hard or innovate, and shortages or surpluses when planners misjudge needs. Mixed economy: advantages are that private firms provide choice and efficiency while the government provides essential services and controls harmful activity; disadvantages are that the taxes needed for public services can discourage enterprise and state-run activities may be inefficient.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A town has privately owned bakeries and publicly provided roads and schools. The town illustrates a mixed arrangement: private producers decide what bread to offer, while public provision supports the community. Market competition may encourage responsiveness and cost control, but people with little purchasing power may not obtain all the services they need. Planning can pursue collective priorities, but planners may lack detailed local information. A comparison should connect a feature to its consequence rather than label one system good in every situation.

blocks.heading: A market economy
blocks.text: In a market economy, resources are mainly privately owned and are allocated through prices (supply and demand), with little government involvement. Producers respond to customers’ willingness and ability to pay.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Two bakers compete for customers in the same town. Competition may encourage a better offer, but people unable to pay may still lack access to what they need.

blocks.heading: A mixed economy
blocks.text: A mixed economy combines private enterprise with public ownership, services and regulation. The balance and form of involvement can differ between places and activities.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A private bakery uses publicly provided roads. The combination illustrates private production supported by public provision; mixed does not mean exactly equal ownership.

blocks.heading: A planned economy
blocks.text: In a planned economy, the government owns most resources and decides centrally what is produced, how it is produced and who receives it; prices play only a small part. Collective priorities guide what is produced and how resources are used.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A public plan assigns output priorities to food producers. The plan can direct resources towards a chosen need, but its usefulness depends on information about local conditions and capacity.
